title: Stitched surface codes: planar concatenation through GHZ corridors
authors: Mohamed A. Shalby, Alexandre Bourassa, Amir Karamlou, Leigh Martin, Alexis Morvan, Nicholas Noll, Craig Gidney, Leonid P. Pryadko
abstract: We present a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture that concatenates four distance-t rotated surface-code patches with the [[4,2,2]] outer code, encoding two logical qubits at code distance d = 2t in a physical footprint of N < 2(2t+1)^2 qubits on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor connectivity. The outer-code stabilizer generators XXXX and ZZZZ, each of physical weight 4t, are measured in situ via verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between adjacent patches, without lattice surgery or long-range gates. The outer-code gadgets introduce hyperedge fault mechanisms, but by design each decomposes into graphlike components, so the complete syndrome is decoded by a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass. Circuit-level simulations show logical error rates that scale as p^t, consistent with distance-2t protection. Finally, we implement the construction experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in both the ZZ and XX memory bases. With the correlated-matching decoder, increasing the code distance from d = 4 to d = 6 reduces the block logical error rate by a factor of 1.52. The construction thus provides a near-term testbed for concatenated architectures beyond the standard surface code.
summary: This work introduces a novel, fault-tolerant quantum memory architecture by stitching together multiple surface-code patches using an outer [[4,2,2]] code. The method uses GHZ ancillae in narrow corridors for syndrome measurement, allowing for efficient decoding via a single matching pass. Experimentally, the construction demonstrates robust error suppression on superconducting hardware, advancing the field toward scalable quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper presents a fault-tolerant quantum-memory architecture by concatenating multiple surface-code patches using an outer [[4,2,2]] code.
main_result: The constructed architecture successfully encodes two logical qubits with distance $d=2t$ while maintaining nearest-neighbor connectivity, showing error rate scaling consistent with theory.
method: The outer-code stabilizers are measured in situ using verified Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) ancillae distributed through narrow corridors between patches, and decoding is achieved via a single minimum-weight-perfect-matching pass.
model_or_system: The system is a stitched surface code composed of four distance-$t$ rotated surface-code patches connected by GHZ corridors, implemented experimentally on a 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor.
key_observables: Logical error rates ($\sim p^t$), block logical error rate reduction factor (1.52 when increasing $d$ from 4 to 6), and detector fire probabilities.
important_parameters: Code distance $d=2t$, physical qubit count $N < 2(2t+1)^2$, and the physical error rate $p$.
main_assumptions: The outer-code gadgets decompose into graphlike components allowing for single MWPM decoding, and the GHZ corridor preparation is constant depth.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the stabilizer structure for $t=3$ showing patches connected by GHZ corridors; other figures compare hardware vs. simulation results for detector probabilities and stability.
paper_structure: The paper details the architecture design, the constant-depth GHZ corridor measurement protocol, the single MWPM decoding scheme, and concludes with experimental validation on superconducting hardware.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, near-term hardware testbed for advanced concatenated quantum error correction beyond the standard surface code, which is highly relevant for experimental quantum information scientists.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Stabilizer structure for the t = 3 stitched code, with four rotated surface-code patches connected by the vertical and horizontal GHZ corridors for the outer-code generators. Filled and open circles, respectively, represent data and an- cillary qubits.

FIG. 2. A single GHZ preparation round for patch distance t = 3, in six time steps (a)–(f). Neighboring corridor qubits are clustered into small GHZ states, intermediate qubits are measured, and the outcomes are absorbed virtually into the detector frame to align the GHZ branches.

FIG. 3. A single GHZ verification round for patch distance t = 3, in six time steps (a)–(f). Pairwise ZZ parities along the corridor are measured by short-depth CNOT circuits using the ancillae on the corridor’s center line, detecting X errors on the GHZ resource state before the transversal CNOT gates couple it to the surface-code patches.

FIG. 4. Logical error rate µtot per surface-code cycle (Sec. V A) versus physical error rate p for patch distance t = 7 under SI1000 noise, with rv = 2–6 GHZ verification rounds (Sec. III B). Solid curves: errors present on all oper- ations (pbulk = pGHZ). Dashed curves: errors present on the GHZ corridor only (pbulk = 0). Dotted lines are guides to the eye ∝p3, p5, p7. Bands are 95% Wilson intervals.

Figure 5 compares the logical error rate of the stitched code against two independent rotated surface- code patches of varying distance under SI1000; Fig. 11 in Appendix C repeats the comparison under the uniform depolarizing model. In both models the stitched code’s logical error rate scales as pt (slope t on log-log axes), consistent with code distance d = 2t.
